newsitem.title: HONG KONG: CEPA tug of war cannot be ruled out.
newsitem.headline: CEPA tug of war cannot be ruled out.

text.p: A tug of war for Hopewell Holdings Ltd's Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd would be surprising but cannot be ruled out said analysts, who tipped Malaysia's YTL Corp Bhd as a possible bidder.

CEPA said on Thursday it had been approached by a third party about a possible acquisition of a controlling stake in the firm just two weeks after Hopewell agreed to sell a major part of CEPA to Southern Co's Southern Electric International. CEPA said a formal offer had not been made by the third party.
"A miracle has come," said Alice Hui, analyst at W.I. Carr.

Southern Electric's HK$18.50 per share offer to acquire a controlling stake in CEPA had already been considered an attractive price for CEPA, analysts said. "I think today's announcement is positive news for both CEPA and Hopewell. It implies a higher bidding price for CEPA shares," said Hui.

Analysts said market rumours were circulating suggesting a Southeast Asian consortium may be interested in a controlling CEPA stake. They pointed to YTL, a Malaysian infrastructure developer and power concern, as a likely potential candidate.
Officials at YTL in Malaysia and Hopewell and CEPA in Hong Kong were not immediately available for comment.
Dominic Armstrong, head of research at Pesaka Jardine Fleming in Kuala Lumpur, said any deal with CEPA would be a "logical extension of their (YTL's) existing business."
"They are a very high profile Malaysian company that has talked about expanding regionally," Armstrong said.
Southern Electric regional director in Hong Kong Ray Harris said the firm was "very hopeful" its deal would go forward.
For Hopewell to back down on the Southern deal, analysts said a new bidder would have to offer a more attractive price.

"It (HK$18.50) was regarded as being an OK price. If it's a higher price then the board has to consider that. They have to have a good reason to reject it," said Howard Gorges, a director at South China Brokerage.
Another analyst said he would be surprised to see Hopewell back down since "it seemed like a fairly concrete deal".
But he said a new bidder only needed 25 percent of CEPA shares to block the vote. Hopewell owns 60.4 percent of CEPA.
"It is feasible that if there is a concrete offer higher then it might not be difficult to convince minority CEPA shareholders to take a higher offer," the analyst said.

Frederick Tsang, head of research at PrimeEast Securities (HK) Ltd, said while a U.S. company may want to spend US$2.7 billion to get a foothold in Asia, he was not so sure a company or consortium already present here would want to.
"It is a very good concept for a U.S. company to have a stake in Asia but if you are already in Asia, I am not so sure."
Analysts said it was difficult to put a valuation on CEPA.
"In a takeover unless you can measure something against assets, or a very clear earnings picture, which you can't for CEPA, then beauty is in the eye of the beholder," said Gorges.

Hui said YTL would have to raise its gearing in order to acquire CEPA. "In terms of financial position, we have to be realistic. So I think if YTL would like to pick up CEPA it will eventually have to gear up itself," she said.
Analysts in Kuala Lumpur said they did not expect YTL to enter into a bidding war for CEPA that would hurt its finances or its good relationship with its shareholders.
Analysts said while they would be surprised to see a counter bid emerge, it could not be ruled out. "Takeover situations aren't over until closed," said Gorges.
